questions.q: What makes production different from every other environment in the hierarchy, per this lesson?
options: Production is the only environment where the cost of a mistake is measured in real business impact, not just developer time
Production cannot be refreshed from any other environment
Production is the only environment that supports Apex code
Production is the only environment that requires a sandbox template
questions.explain: A mistake in a development or testing environment costs time to fix; a mistake in production can mean real broken reports, failed integrations, or corrupted data affecting the actual business.

questions.q: What is the core hygiene rule this lesson teaches about production?
options: Changes should always be built and validated directly in production because it's the most realistic environment
Changes are built and validated elsewhere in the promotion path, and only ever deployed into production -- never built there directly
Production should never be used by any Salesforce user
Production changes don't need any review as long as they're small
questions.explain: This is the entire reason the development, testing, and staging tiers exist -- bypassing them to build directly in production removes the promotion path's safety guarantee for that change.

questions.q: What does "change control" refer to in a production context?
options: A Salesforce feature that automatically blocks all metadata changes
A once-a-year audit of all production users
The process of renaming fields in production
Practices that keep every production change traceable, reviewed by someone other than the person making it, and reversible
questions.explain: Change control covers traceability (a record of what changed and when), independent review before deployment, and the ability to reverse a change -- not a one-time audit.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a production hygiene failure doesn't stay contained to production alone?
options: Because production automatically emails every admin when a change is made
Because Salesforce deletes all sandboxes if production has an error
Because every other environment is eventually refreshed from production, so undocumented configuration that bypassed the promotion path propagates downstream into sandboxes refreshed afterward
Because production and every sandbox share the exact same storage at all times
questions.explain: A Full or Partial Copy sandbox refresh pulls from production -- so an undocumented change made directly in production reappears in the very environments meant to catch problems before they reach production.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a real rollback plan requires, as distinct from "we'll figure out how to undo this if it breaks"?
options: Deleting the production org and recreating it from a sandbox
Nothing -- rollback plans are only needed for changes that fail in staging
A rollback plan is only required for changes made by contractors, not employees
Knowing in advance, before deploying, the specific way a given release would be undone -- such as reverting a package version or restoring from backup
questions.explain: A mature production practice defines the specific undo mechanism for a release before deploying it -- deciding this only after something breaks is not a rollback plan.
